Triggers.value: People who are related to the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
I can't stop bad things from happening to me
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Bao had always believed his role as a hospital chaplain was to be a steady presence in the chaos, a calm anchor for families adrift in grief and fear. For the past six months, however, he had felt like a fraud. At thirty-four, he was a man hollowed out by a private terror, one that began on a cold Tuesday night on the subway platform. He had been heading home late after sitting with a family whose patriarch had just passed. The platform was dense with the evening rush, a river of bodies he'd navigated a thousand times. But that night, two young men broke from the current, pinning him against a tiled pillar. The memory never came back as a fluid story, only as a series of searing, silent snapshots: the cracked screen of his phone as it hit the ground, the glint of a small blade under the fluorescent lights, the contemptuous sneer on one man's face. He remembered the smell most vividly-a cloying mix of stale cigarette smoke and cheap, sharp cologne that seemed to cling to the back of his throat. And the sound: their ragged, heavy breathing, loud and animalistic in his ear.

In the weeks that followed, these fragments began to intrude on his life with vicious regularity. While counseling a patient, he would suddenly see the blade, not the crucifix on the wall. The scent of a visitor's aftershave would transport him back to the grimy platform, and a wave of nausea would rise in his chest. But what truly frightened him was the rage. When the images came, a white-hot fury would surge through him, so intense he'd have to grip the arms of his chair, his knuckles white, praying it wouldn't show on his face. This wasn't him. He was a man of peace, a widower who had learned to meet profound loss with grace. This new anger felt like a poison.

He came to believe the attack was a judgment on his character. A stronger man, a more vigilant man, would have seen them coming. He would replay the moments leading up to it, convinced that his own softness, the very quality he cultivated as a chaplain, had marked him as a target. He was certain that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation; they would have been tougher, more aware. This conviction fed a deeper, more painful belief that had taken root after his wife's long illness: he was fundamentally helpless, a man to whom bad things simply happened, a person incapable of stopping them.

His world began to shrink. He stopped taking the subway entirely, adding an hour to his commute. The hospital, once his sanctuary, became a landscape of threats. The crowded lobby felt suffocating, each person a potential source of danger. He'd find himself scanning faces, his heart hammering whenever he saw a young man in a hoodie who resembled one of the attackers. The most insidious trigger was the sound of heavy breathing. In a place filled with the sounds of struggle and life-support machines, it was everywhere. Standing by the bedside of a patient with pneumonia, the rhythmic rasp of their breath would send a jolt of pure panic through him, forcing him to cut his visit short with a mumbled excuse. His supervisor noticed his new preference for the quieter oncology ward and his avoidance of the chaotic emergency room, a change so out of character that she had gently asked if everything was alright. It was after that conversation, staring at his own haunted reflection in a window, that Bao knew he could no longer carry the weight of his silent war alone. He was terrified that the calm, compassionate man he had worked so hard to be was being irrevocably consumed by the angry, frightened stranger who now lived inside his skin.
